headline: Network & Cloud Engineer | Routing & Switching | AWS | Linux
summary: Electronics and Communications Engineering graduate with networking depth (CCNA curriculum and Huawei HCIA-Datacom course, studied) applied in the cloud: multi-AZ VPC design, private subnets behind NAT, default-deny security groups, a WireGuard VPN with per-team address ranges and a Squid proxy. Designed a two-floor building network in Cisco Packet Tracer; familiar with routing and switching (OSPF, BGP) and MPLS.

bullets.text: Completed intensive hands-on training in Linux administration, networking, CI/CD, containerization, and cloud infrastructure, culminating in end-to-end DevOps projects (see Projects).
Applied DevOps best practices to production-tier projects, covering CI/CD, GitOps, containerization, and infrastructure automation.

bullets.label: Infrastructure & Access
bullets.text: Enterprise-style RHEL environment on EC2 (VPN gateway, control, identity, utility and per-team workstations) in private subnets behind a NAT gateway, built with modular Terraform; reachable only through a WireGuard VPN with per-team ranges, firewalld and default-deny security groups.

bullets.label: Identity & Team Policy
bullets.text: FreeIPA centralizes users, DNS, Kerberos, HBAC and sudo rules per team; the utility server runs a Squid proxy with per-team internet rules, NFS home directories, centralized logging and backups.

bullets.label: Platform & Security
bullets.text: Five Python/FastAPI banking microservices and an NGINX frontend on EKS, built for financial correctness (fencing tokens, row-lock ordering). Versioned Terraform modules deploy through GitHub Actions (OIDC) and ArgoCD App-of-Apps, secured with default-deny NetworkPolicies, Istio mTLS, Gateway API and External Secrets Operator (IRSA).

bullets.label: Delivery, Streaming & Reliability
bullets.text: Trivy-scanned, Cosign-signed images are promoted by GitOps PRs and released as Argo Rollouts canaries gated on Prometheus metrics. Strimzi Kafka (KRaft, TLS/SCRAM, ACLs, dead-letter queue) carries events; Pytest concurrency tests, Prometheus/Grafana/Loki observability, and a disaster recovery drill rebuilt the cluster in 23 min 50 s with Multi-AZ RDS.
Designed the network for a two-floor building in Cisco Packet Tracer using routers, switches and end devices.

Modular Terraform for a 3-tier AWS app (VPC, ALBs, Auto Scaling groups, RDS) with tier-isolated security groups, deployed through a Jenkins pipeline with a manual approval gate and monitored by CloudWatch alarms.
Three-tier app on Kubernetes secured with RBAC, default-deny NetworkPolicies, and Cilium FQDN-based egress rules, with Ingress and autoscaling.

paragraphs: I am applying for the Network Back Office Engineer role at Orbitel Networks. I combine network fundamentals from my engineering degree with hands-on cloud network design, and I would like to apply both to the day-to-day running of your network.

On routing and switching, my base is the CCNA curriculum and the Huawei HCIA-Datacom course, which I studied, plus a two-floor building network I designed in Cisco Packet Tracer with routers, switches and end devices. My working level with OSPF, BGP and MPLS (L2/L3 VPN, VRF) is familiar rather than production, and I say so plainly. The hands-on side is in my Linux lab on AWS: private subnets behind a NAT gateway, default-deny security groups per role, and a WireGuard VPN carried inside TLS on TCP 443 with per-team ranges that reach only what each team's policy allows. A Squid proxy applies per-team internet rules on top.

My degree and networking courses gave me the fundamentals; building VPNs, proxies and segmented VPCs on AWS showed me how much of reliability and security is decided in the network. The lab also taught me to document changes through tickets, runbooks and incident reports, which fits back office work. My CV is attached, and I would welcome a conversation about how I can contribute.

why_this_role: Designing a two-floor network in Packet Tracer and then building a WireGuard VPN, NAT and segmented VPCs on AWS showed me that network reliability and security start with solid routing and switching fundamentals.
